nameStory: Prairie Junegrass gets its name from its preference for open prairie-like habitats and its peak growing season in June when it produces its delicate flower clusters. The 'prairie' part of the name reflects its love of sunny, open spaces rather than shaded woodlands. In the UK, it's called crested hair-grass because of the fine, hair-like appearance of its flower clusters.
description: Prairie Junegrass is a delicate, clump-forming grass that grows in neat tufts about 1-2 feet tall. It has narrow, blue-green leaves and produces soft, silvery flower clusters that shimmer in the breeze during early summer. This graceful grass forms small bunches rather than spreading into large patches, giving it a refined appearance in the landscape. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special for grass enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces dense, spike-like clusters of tiny flowers that are silvery-white to pale yellow and feel soft to the touch, almost like a bottle brush but more delicate

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow blue-green blades that are flat and smooth, growing mostly from the base in a fountain-like clump with few stem leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinct, neat tufts or bunches rather than spreading widely, creating a tidy clumping appearance about 12-24 inches tall

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, light-colored seeds develop after flowering, remaining attached in the distinctive spike-like seed head through late summer

habitat: In New England, Prairie Junegrass is found in dry, open areas like sandy fields, rocky slopes, and prairie remnants with well-drained soils. It prefers full sun and thrives in somewhat poor, alkaline soils where other grasses might struggle. Look for it in disturbed areas, old fields, or along sunny roadsides where the soil isn't too rich or moist.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge early, forming the characteristic blue-green tufts as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the distinctive silvery flower spikes appear in June and July, making the plant most noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads persist and turn golden-brown, while the leaves may take on autumn tints before going dormant.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried seed stalks and the crown of the plant at soil surface.

funFact: Despite being called 'Prairie' Junegrass, this resilient little grass actually grows on multiple continents and can survive in some of the harshest conditions on Earth, from Arctic tundra to desert edges, making it one of the most widely distributed grasses in the world.
confusionNotes: Prairie Junegrass can be confused with other small bunch grasses, but its distinctive silvery, dense flower spikes that feel soft to the touch set it apart from most others. Remember: if it forms neat clumps and has bottle-brush-like silvery flowers in June, you've likely found Prairie Junegrass.
contextualKnowledge: This grass is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so any potential sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists. It's much more common in western North America, making its presence in New England quite remarkable and worthy of documentation.
compareHints: Prairie Junegrass differs from its relative spike trisetum by having denser, more compact flower clusters and a more distinctly clumping growth habit. While both are bunch grasses, Prairie Junegrass has a softer, more silvery appearance to its seed heads, whereas spike trisetum tends to have a more open, loose flower arrangement. Prairie Junegrass also tends to be shorter and more compact overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spike trisetum differs from its close relative prairie junegrass by having more compact, denser flower clusters and narrower leaves.
